SELLING STOCK, LLC INTERESTS, OR INVESTOR NOTES WITHOUT QUALIFYING — CORPORATIONS CODE § 25110 AND THE BUYER'S RESCISSION REMEDY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jane Doe, states what California law provides about the requirement that a security be qualified before it is offered or sold in this state, about which interests in a business count as “securities” for that purpose, and about the civil, procedural, and criminal consequences California law attaches to an offer or sale that is neither qualified nor exempt. The interests it concerns are the ordinary instruments of business formation and early financing — shares of stock, limited liability company membership interests, limited and general partnership and joint venture interests, promissory notes given to investors, and interests in a profit-sharing arrangement — issued by Acme, Inc. or by any other issuer. Where a specific business name appears below, that is Acme, Inc.; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what these statutes and decisions say. This sheet states the law. It does not evaluate whether any particular interest issued by Acme, Inc. is a security, whether any exemption applies to any particular offer or sale, or whether any person is liable for anything, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

THE QUALIFICATION REQUIREMENT FOR AN ISSUER'S OWN SECURITIES
California Corporations Code § 25110, part of the Corporate Securities Law of 1968, makes it unlawful for any person to offer or sell a security in this state in an “issuer transaction” — the transaction in which the issuing business itself sells its own securities, as distinct from a later resale by a holder — unless one of two things is true: the sale has been qualified with the state under Section 25111, 25112, or 25113 and no stop order is in effect, or the security or the transaction is exempted from, or not subject to, qualification under the exemption chapter that begins at Section 25100. The statute reaches an offer as well as a sale, and it applies whether or not underwriters are involved. A second sentence of the same section addresses offerings that were qualified but then conducted differently: an offer or sale made in a manner that varies or differs from, exceeds the scope of, or fails to conform with a material term or material condition of the qualification — or a material representation about the manner of offering set out in the qualification application — is itself an unqualified offer or sale.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "It is unlawful for any person to offer or sell in this state any security in an issuer transaction (other than in a transaction subject to Section 25120), whether or not by or through underwriters, unless such sale has been qualified under Section 25111, 25112 or 25113 (and no order under Section 25140 or subdivision (a) of Section 25143 is in effect with respect to such qualification) or unless such security or transaction is exempted or not subject to qualification under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 25100) of this part."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25110, California Corporations Code, Corporate Securities Law of 1968 — qualification requirement for issuer transactions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25110.)
  "The offer or sale of such a security in a manner that varies or differs from, exceeds the scope of, or fails to conform with either a material term or material condition of qualification of the offering as set forth in the permit or qualification order, or a material representation as to the manner of offering which is set forth in the application for qualification, shall be an unqualified offer or sale."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25110, California Corporations Code § 25110, second sentence — offerings that depart from the terms of qualification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25110.)
  Known gap: This clause states the rule for issuer transactions under Section 25110 only. The Corporate Securities Law imposes parallel, separately worded qualification requirements on other kinds of transactions that this document does not address — Section 25120 (recapitalizations, reorganizations, and similar changes in rights) and Section 25130 (non-issuer transactions). The section's cross-references to Sections 25111, 25112, 25113, 25140, 25143, and to the exemption chapter beginning at Section 25100 are not themselves quoted or summarized here; the many separate exemptions in that chapter, including the limited offering exemption of Section 25102(f) covered by a separate document in this collection, each carry their own conditions. California qualification is also separate from, and additional to, registration under the federal Securities Act of 1933, which this clause does not address. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular offer or sale has been qualified or is exempt.

WHAT THE STATUTE COUNTS AS A “SECURITY”
The reach of the qualification requirement depends on the statutory definition of “security” in Corporations Code § 25019, which is a long enumerated list rather than a general standard. Among the instruments it names are any note, stock, treasury stock, membership in an incorporated or unincorporated association, bond, debenture, evidence of indebtedness, certificate of interest or participation in any profit-sharing agreement, preorganization certificate or subscription, transferable share, and investment contract. The list separately names an interest in a limited liability company, and any class or series of those interests, with one exception: a membership interest is outside the definition where the person claiming the exception can prove that all of the members are actively engaged in the management of the company. The same sentence limits that exception — evidence that members vote or have the right to vote, or have the right to information about the company's business and affairs, or have the right to participate in management, does not establish without more that all members are actively engaged in management. The section closes the list with a catchall for any interest or instrument commonly known as a “security,” and states that all of the listed items are securities whether or not evidenced by a written document. The section also excludes four categories outright, including a beneficial interest in a voluntary inter vivos trust not created to carry on a business, and a franchise subject to registration under the Franchise Investment Law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Security” means any note; stock; treasury stock; membership in an incorporated or unincorporated association; bond; debenture; evidence of indebtedness; certificate of interest or participation in any profit-sharing agreement; collateral trust certificate; preorganization certificate or subscription; transferable share; investment contract;"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25019, California Corporations Code, Corporate Securities Law of 1968 — definition of “security” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25019.)
  "interest in a limited liability company and any class or series of those interests (including any fractional or other interest in that interest), except a membership interest in a limited liability company in which the person claiming this exception can prove that all of the members are actively engaged in the management of the limited liability company; provided that evidence that members vote or have the right to vote, or the right to information concerning the business and affairs of the limited liability company, or the right to participate in management, shall not establish, without more, that all members are actively engaged in the management of the limited liability company;"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25019, California Corporations Code § 25019 — limited liability company interests and the active-management exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25019.)
  "or, in general, any interest or instrument commonly known as a “security”; or any certificate of interest or participation in, temporary or interim certificate for, receipt for, guarantee of, or warrant or right to subscribe to or purchase, any of the foregoing. All of the foregoing are securities whether or not evidenced by a written document."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25019, California Corporations Code § 25019 — catchall and no-writing-required sentence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25019.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes three separate passages of a single statutory section, Corporations Code § 25019; they are parts of one source, not independent authorities. The quoted material is not the whole section — the definition also names collateral trust certificates, viatical and life settlement contracts, voting trust certificates, certificates of deposit for a security, oil, gas, and mining interests, puts, calls, straddles, options, and privileges, and interests issued in connection with funded employee benefit plans, none of which are quoted here. The four exclusions at the end of the section are summarized in part and not quoted. The statute does not define “investment contract” or “actively engaged in the management”; the case law that supplies the test for an investment contract appears in the following clauses. This clause does not determine whether any particular instrument or interest is a security.

THE TWO TESTS CALIFORNIA COURTS USE FOR AN “INVESTMENT CONTRACT”
Because “investment contract” is one of the instruments listed in the statutory definition, an arrangement that carries none of the familiar labels can still be a security. In Silver Hills Country Club v. Sobieski, the California Supreme Court held that memberships sold to finance the development of a country club were securities, reasoning that the sellers were soliciting risk capital with which to develop a business for profit and that the purchaser's risk was not lessened by the label put on what he bought. That reasoning became known as the risk capital test. Decades later, in People v. Figueroa, the Supreme Court described Silver Hills as having introduced the concept of “risk capital” as a way to determine whether a transaction involves a security, and observed in the same discussion that an investor who entrusts money to a promoter but retains substantial power to affect the success of the enterprise has not risked capital within the meaning of the Corporate Securities Law. The Court of Appeal in Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations collected the current framework: California courts have applied, either separately or together, two distinct tests — the risk capital test of Silver Hills and the federal test of SEC v. W. J. Howey Co., under which an investment contract is an arrangement whereby a person invests money in a common enterprise and is led to expect profits solely from the efforts of the promoter or a third party — and a transaction is a security if it satisfies either test.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "We have here nothing like the ordinary sale of a right to use existing facilities. Petitioners are soliciting the risk capital with which to develop a business for profit. The purchaser’s risk is not lessened merely because the interest he purchases is labelled a membership."
  — Silver Hills Country Club v. Sobieski (1961) 55 Cal.2d 811, 55 Cal.2d 811, 815 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1296034/silver-hills-country-club-v-sobieski/)
  "Some 25 years ago, this court in Silver Hills Country Club v. Sobieski, supra, 55 Cal.2d 811 introduced the concept of “risk capital” as a way to determine whether a transaction involves a “security.”"
  — People v. Figueroa (1986) 41 Cal.3d 714, 41 Cal.3d 714, 736-737 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1387758/people-v-figueroa/)
  "retains substantial power to affect the success of the enterprise, he has not “risked capital” within the meaning of the Corporate Securities Law."
  — People v. Figueroa (1986) 41 Cal.3d 714, 41 Cal.3d 714, 739 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1387758/people-v-figueroa/)
  "In determining whether a transaction is an investment contract, California courts have applied, either separately or together, two distinct tests:"
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 609-610 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  "A transaction is a security if it satisfies either test."
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 610 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  "Under the federal test, an investment contract is “a contract, transaction or scheme whereby a person invests his money in a common enterprise and is led to expect profits solely from the efforts of the promoter or a third party.”"
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 610 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  Known gap: Silver Hills was decided in 1961 under the predecessor Corporate Securities Act, and the sentence quoted from it refers to “Section 25008,” which was then the definition of “security”; under the Corporate Securities Law of 1968 the definition is at Section 25019 and Section 25008 now governs when an offer or sale is made in this state. The two later decisions quoted here are cited for the continuing use of the risk capital test under the current law. The Consolidated Management court was quoting its own earlier decision in Reiswig v. Department of Corporations (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 327, 334, and the federal test it described comes from SEC v. W. J. Howey Co. (1946) 328 U.S. 293; neither of those decisions was independently fetched for this document. Consolidated Management resolved the case under the federal test and expressly did not decide whether the risk capital test was also satisfied. The passage quoted from Figueroa about retained power appears in the fetched text immediately after a reporter page break within the sentence, so the quotation below begins mid-sentence at the start of page 739 rather than reproducing the full sentence. This clause does not apply either test to any particular arrangement.

WHEN A PARTNERSHIP, JOINT VENTURE, OR LLC INTEREST IS TREATED AS A SECURITY
Ownership interests in unincorporated businesses sit on both sides of the line. In Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations, the Court of Appeal adopted a securities treatise's statement that the pivotal criterion for distinguishing partnership or joint venture interests — and limited liability company membership interests — that are securities from those that are not is usually the “solely [or substantially] from the efforts of others” element of the federal test: where profits are to come substantially from the efforts of others, as in the typical limited partnership, a security will be present, while where profits are to come from the joint efforts of the partners, as in the typical general partnership, a security usually will not be present. The same decision adopted the federal Williamson v. Tucker framework for interests that carry the general-partnership form: the investor bears the burden of showing that, despite that form, the investor was so dependent on the promoter or a third party as to be in fact unable to exercise meaningful partnership powers, which may be established, for example, by an agreement leaving so little power in the partner's hands that power is in fact distributed as it would be in a limited partnership, by the partner's inexperience and lack of knowledge in business affairs, or by dependence on some unique entrepreneurial or managerial ability of the promoter or manager. The court added that other factors could also show such dependence, and that the focus is on investor expectations at the time of the original investment. This case-law framework runs alongside the statutory text discussed above, under which an LLC interest is listed as a security unless the person claiming the exception proves that all members are actively engaged in management.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Where profits are to come substantially from the efforts of others (the typical case in a limited partnership), a security will be present. On the other hand, where profits are to come from the joint efforts of partners (the typical case in a general partnership), a security usually will not be present."
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 610 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  "demonstrate that, in spite of the partnership form which the investment took, he was so dependent on the promoter or on a third party that he was in fact unable to exercise meaningful partnership powers."
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 611 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  "A general partnership or joint venture interest can be designated a security if the investor can establish, for example, that (1) an agreement among the parties leaves so little power in the hands of the partner or venturer that the arrangement in fact distributes power as would a limited partnership; or (2) the partner or venturer is so inexperienced and unknowledgeable in business affairs that he is incapable of intelligently exercising his partnership or venture powers; or (3) the partner or venturer is so dependent on some unique entrepreneurial or managerial ability of the promoter or manager that he cannot replace the manager of the enterprise or otherwise exercise meaningful partnership or venture powers."
  — Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 162 Cal.App.4th 598, 611 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2291082/consolidated-management-group-v-department-of-corporations/)
  Known gap: The first passage quoted below is the Consolidated Management court quoting a securities treatise (II Loss et al., Securities Regulation (4th ed. 2007) pp. 985-986), and the second is that court quoting Williamson v. Tucker (5th Cir. 1981) 645 F.2d 404, 424, a federal decision construing the federal securities laws; neither the treatise nor Williamson was independently fetched for this document, and the quotations are verified as they appear in the California decision's text. Consolidated Management applied this framework to Kansas joint venture interests offered to California investors and held the interests were securities; its statements about limited liability company interests were made in the course of describing the general criterion rather than in deciding an LLC case. The Williamson factors are stated in the decision as examples, not as an exhaustive list, and federal circuits have applied the second factor differently, a split the decision itself notes. This clause does not determine whether any particular partnership, joint venture, or membership interest is a security.

WHEN AN OFFER OR SALE IS MADE “IN THIS STATE”
Section 25110 applies to an offer or sale made “in this state,” and Corporations Code § 25008 supplies the test for that phrase rather than leaving it to the parties' descriptions of the deal. An offer or sale of a security is made in this state when an offer to sell is made in this state, when an offer to buy is accepted in this state, or — if both the seller and the purchaser are domiciled in this state — when the security is delivered to the purchaser in this state. The same section then defines those component events: an offer to sell or to buy is made in this state when the offer either originates from this state or is directed by the offeror to this state and received at the place to which it is directed, and an offer is accepted in this state when acceptance is communicated to the offeror in this state. A separate subdivision provides that an offer is not made in this state merely because a bona fide newspaper or other publication of general, regular, and paid circulation with more than two-thirds of its circulation outside California over the past 12 months is circulated here, or because a radio or television program originating outside the state is received here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "An offer or sale of a security is made in this state when an offer to sell is made in this state, or an offer to buy is accepted in this state, or (if both the seller and the purchaser are domiciled in this state) the security is delivered to the purchaser in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25008(a), California Corporations Code — when an offer or sale of a security is made in this state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25008.)
  "An offer to sell or to buy is made in this state when the offer either originates from this state or is directed by the offeror to this state and received at the place to which it is directed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25008(b), California Corporations Code — when an offer is made in, or accepted in, this state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25008.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on the single section that supplies the territorial test, Corporations Code § 25008; subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) are parts of that one section rather than independent sources. The section was enacted in 1968 and addresses offers communicated by mail, telephone, radio, and television; it does not by its terms address internet or electronic communications, and this clause does not extend it to them. Section 25008 governs where an offer or sale occurs; it does not decide whether the thing offered is a security or whether an exemption applies. This clause does not determine where any particular offer or sale was made.

WHO MUST PROVE AN EXEMPTION
The qualification requirement is written as a prohibition subject to exemptions, and California law places the burden of establishing an exemption on the party who relies on it. Corporations Code § 25163 provides that in any proceeding under the Corporate Securities Law, the burden of proving an exemption or an exception from a definition is upon the person claiming it. The section is not limited to civil actions, and by its terms it covers both exemptions from qualification and exceptions written into the statutory definitions — for example, the limited liability company active-management exception in the definition of “security,” which the definition itself frames as something the person claiming it must prove.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In any proceeding under this law, the burden of proving an exemption or an exception from a definition is upon the person claiming it."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25163, California Corporations Code — burden of proving an exemption or an exception from a definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25163.)
  Known gap: Corporations Code § 25163 is a single sentence and the sole source cited for this clause; no independent authority is quoted here for how the burden operates in a particular procedural posture. The section allocates the burden of proof but says nothing about the standard of proof, which differs between civil and criminal proceedings, and this clause does not state what that standard is in either setting. The exemptions themselves — the securities exemptions and transaction exemptions in the chapter beginning at Section 25100, including Section 25102(f) — are not listed or described here. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular exemption is available to anyone.

THE BUYER'S CIVIL REMEDY FOR AN UNQUALIFIED SALE
Corporations Code § 25503 creates a private remedy running to the purchaser. A person who violates Section 25110 (among other listed provisions) is liable to any person who acquired the security from them in violation of that section, and that buyer may sue to recover the consideration paid for the security, with interest at the legal rate and reasonable attorney's fees, less any income received from the security, upon tender of the security back to the seller — or for damages instead, if the buyer no longer owns the security or if the consideration given cannot be returned. The statute then sets out how damages are measured in each of those situations, and provides that any tender required by the section may be made at any time before entry of judgment. Liability under the section does not turn on the seller's intent or on any misstatement about the business; the violation is the unqualified offer or sale itself. The section also contains a curative provision: no person is liable under it for a violation of Section 25110, 25120, or 25130 if the sale of the security is qualified before any part of the consideration for the security sold is paid or received, even though an offer to sell or a contract of sale may have been made without qualification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Any person who violates Section 25110, 25130, or 25133, or a condition of qualification under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 25110) of this part, imposed pursuant to Section 25141, or an order suspending trading issued pursuant to Section 25219, shall be liable to any person acquiring from them the security sold in violation of that section, who may sue to recover the consideration they paid for that security with interest thereon at the legal rate, and reasonable attorney’s fees, less the amount of any income received therefrom, upon the tender of that security, or for damages, if they no longer own the security, or if the consideration given for the security is not capable of being returned."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25503, California Corporations Code — civil liability for sale of an unqualified security (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25503.)
  "Any tender specified in this section may be made at any time before entry of judgment. No person shall be liable under this section for violation of Section 25110, 25120 or 25130 if the sale of the security is qualified prior to the payment or receipt of any part of the consideration for the security sold, even though an offer to sell or a contract of sale may have been made or entered into without qualification."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25503, California Corporations Code § 25503 — tender before judgment and qualification before consideration is paid (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25503.)
  Known gap: The two passages quoted below are parts of the same statutory section, Corporations Code § 25503, and are not independent sources. The section's detailed damages formulas — for a plaintiff who no longer owns the security and for a plaintiff whose consideration cannot be returned — are summarized rather than quoted, as are its separate provisions on liability for violations of Section 25120 and on the joint and several liability and damages cap applicable to underwriters. The statement in the body that liability does not depend on the seller's intent reflects the absence of any intent element in the quoted text of Section 25503 and Section 25110; no case is cited here for that reading. Statutes governing when such an action must be brought, and a procedure by which a written rescission offer can bar suit, appear in a later clause of this document. This clause does not evaluate whether anyone has a claim or a defense.

OTHERS WHO CAN BE LIABLE ALONGSIDE THE SELLER
Liability for an unqualified sale is not confined to the entity that issued the security. Corporations Code § 25504 makes a defined group jointly and severally liable, to the same extent as the person primarily liable under Section 25503: every person who directly or indirectly controls that person, every partner in a firm so liable, every principal executive officer or director of a corporation so liable, every person occupying a similar status or performing similar functions, every employee of a person so liable who materially aids in the act or transaction constituting the violation, and every broker-dealer or agent who materially aids in it. The section supplies its own defense: a person in that group is not liable if that person had no knowledge of, or reasonable grounds to believe in the existence of, the facts by reason of which the liability is alleged to exist. A separate section, Corporations Code § 25504.1, reaches more broadly but requires a culpable state of mind — any person who materially assists in a violation of Section 25110 (among other provisions) with intent to deceive or defraud is jointly and severally liable with any other person liable for that violation.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25504, California Corporations Code — joint and several liability of controlling persons, officers, directors, employees, and agents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25504.)

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25504.1, California Corporations Code — liability of a person who materially assists with intent to deceive or defraud (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25504.1.)
  Known gap: Sections 25504 and 25504.1 are separate statutory sections but sit in the same chapter of the Corporate Securities Law and are quoted from the same fetched chapter text; they are not independent authorities for each other. Neither section defines “controls,” “materially aids,” or “materially assists,” and this clause does not supply definitions or cite case law construing those terms. Section 25504.2, which addresses accountants, engineers, appraisers, and other professionals named in an offering document, and the remaining provisions of the same chapter are not covered here. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular officer, director, employee, partner, or adviser falls within either section.

THE TIME LIMIT ON SUIT AND THE STATUTORY RESCISSION OFFER
Corporations Code § 25507 does two things to the remedy created by Section 25503. First, subdivision (a) sets the time limit: no action may be maintained to enforce a liability created under Section 25503 (or under Sections 25504 or 25504.1 insofar as they relate to it) unless brought before the expiration of two years after the violation on which it is based, or the expiration of one year after the plaintiff's discovery of the facts constituting the violation, whichever expires first. Second, subdivision (b) provides a way for a seller to cut off the claim before suit: a buyer may not commence an action under those sections if, before suit, the buyer received a written offer, approved as to form by the Commissioner, that states the respect in which liability may have arisen, offers either to repurchase the security for cash or to pay the amount recoverable under Section 25503 or to rescind the transaction by putting the parties back in the same position as before, remains open for a specified period of not less than 30 days after receipt, sets forth subdivision (b) itself, and contains any other information the Commissioner requires — and the buyer failed to accept that offer in writing within the specified period. Subdivision (c) lets the Commissioner impose conditions on approval of such an offer, including that equivalent and concurrent offers be made to all investors as to whom liability may have arisen and still exists.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25507(a), California Corporations Code — two-year and one-year limits on an action under Section 25503 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25507.)
  "No buyer may commence an action under Section 25503 (or Section 25504 or Section 25504.1 insofar as they relate to that section) if, before suit is commenced, such buyer shall have received a written offer approved as to form by the commissioner"

  Known gap: Subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) quoted or summarized here are parts of a single section, Corporations Code § 25507, not independent sources. The section refers to the “commissioner”; the office administering the Corporate Securities Law has been renamed over time and is now within the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation, and no separate source is cited here for that renaming. This clause does not address the separate limitations provisions that govern other liabilities created by the Corporate Securities Law, such as Section 25506 for claims under Section 25500 or 25501, and it does not address tolling, delayed discovery beyond the statutory text, or any other doctrine that might affect the running of the period. It does not evaluate whether any particular claim is timely or whether any particular offer satisfies subdivision (b).

WILLFUL VIOLATIONS AS A CRIME, AND THE JURY'S ROLE IN DECIDING WHAT IS A SECURITY
The Corporate Securities Law also carries criminal penalties. Corporations Code § 25540(a) provides that, except as provided in subdivision (b), any person who willfully violates any provision of the division — which includes the qualification requirement of Section 25110 — or who willfully violates any rule or order under it, is upon conviction subject to a fine of not more than one million dollars, or imprisonment under subdivision (h) of Penal Code Section 1170 or in a county jail for not more than one year, or both; and no person may be imprisoned for violating a rule or order if that person proves no knowledge of the rule or order. People v. Figueroa was such a prosecution: the defendants appealed from a judgment of conviction for one count of selling unqualified securities under Sections 25110 and 25540. California Corporations Code § 25110, part of the Corporate Securities Law of 1968, makes it unlawful for any person to offer or sell a security in this state in an “issuer transaction” — the transaction in which the issuing business itself sells its own securities, as distinct from a later resale by a holder — unless one of two things is true: the sale has been qualified with the state under Section 25111, 25112, or 25113 and no stop order is in effect, or the security or the transaction is exempted from, or not subject to, qualification under the exemption chapter that begins at Section 25100. The statute reaches an offer as well as a sale, and it applies whether or not underwriters are involved. A second sentence of the same section addresses offerings that were qualified but then conducted differently: an offer or sale made in a manner that varies or differs from, exceeds the scope of, or fails to conform with a material term or material condition of the qualification — or a material representation about the manner of offering set out in the qualification application — is itself an unqualified offer or sale.

expectedJSON.body: Because “investment contract” is one of the instruments listed in the statutory definition, an arrangement that carries none of the familiar labels can still be a security. In Silver Hills Country Club v. Sobieski, the California Supreme Court held that memberships sold to finance the development of a country club were securities, reasoning that the sellers were soliciting risk capital with which to develop a business for profit and that the purchaser's risk was not lessened by the label put on what he bought. That reasoning became known as the risk capital test. Decades later, in People v. Figueroa, the Supreme Court described Silver Hills as having introduced the concept of “risk capital” as a way to determine whether a transaction involves a security, and observed in the same discussion that an investor who entrusts money to a promoter but retains substantial power to affect the success of the enterprise has not risked capital within the meaning of the Corporate Securities Law. The Court of Appeal in Consolidated Management Group, LLC v. Department of Corporations collected the current framework: California courts have applied, either separately or together, two distinct tests — the risk capital test of Silver Hills and the federal test of SEC v. W. J. Howey Co., under which an investment contract is an arrangement whereby a person invests money in a common enterprise and is led to expect profits solely from the efforts of the promoter or a third party — and a transaction is a security if it satisfies either test.

The same decision adopted the federal Williamson v. expectedJSON.body: Section 25110 applies to an offer or sale made “in this state,” and Corporations Code § 25008 supplies the test for that phrase rather than leaving it to the parties' descriptions of the deal. An offer or sale of a security is made in this state when an offer to sell is made in this state, when an offer to buy is accepted in this state, or — if both the seller and the purchaser are domiciled in this state — when the security is delivered to the purchaser in this state. The same section then defines those component events: an offer to sell or to buy is made in this state when the offer either originates from this state or is directed by the offeror to this state and received at the place to which it is directed, and an offer is accepted in this state when acceptance is communicated to the offeror in this state. A separate subdivision provides that an offer is not made in this state merely because a bona fide newspaper or other publication of general, regular, and paid circulation with more than two-thirds of its circulation outside California over the past 12 months is circulated here, or because a radio or television program originating outside the state is received here.

expectedJSON.body: Corporations Code § 25503 creates a private remedy running to the purchaser. A person who violates Section 25110 (among other listed provisions) is liable to any person who acquired the security from them in violation of that section, and that buyer may sue to recover the consideration paid for the security, with interest at the legal rate and reasonable attorney's fees, less any income received from the security, upon tender of the security back to the seller — or for damages instead, if the buyer no longer owns the security or if the consideration given cannot be returned. The statute then sets out how damages are measured in each of those situations, and provides that any tender required by the section may be made at any time before entry of judgment. Liability under the section does not turn on the seller's intent or on any misstatement about the business; the violation is the unqualified offer or sale itself. The section also contains a curative provision: no person is liable under it for a violation of Section 25110, 25120, or 25130 if the sale of the security is qualified before any part of the consideration for the security sold is paid or received, even though an offer to sell or a contract of sale may have been made without qualification.
